whatItFakes: An outlet's revenue (its audience's subscriptions and the advertising they see) is one standing monthly payment from the town's outside customers. It is re-sized each month to the outlet's audience now and its people's cost (src/core2/press-money.ts), but local businesses still buy no ads, households' own reading spending still goes to the outside account, and the payer is not the readers or the advertisers by name. The estimate also anchors employer demand; nonpayroll supplier contracts are not modeled.
why: Local advertising needs businesses that choose to advertise, which the business engine (OPUS-WORLD) does not model; the outlet's people must be paid from its own cash now.
replacement: Resolved: an outlet's revenue is its readers' subscriptions, paid from each reader household's living cost (the counted households by the same rule times their readers), and the ads the town's businesses buy from their own outside costs, on a sliding scale to their cash and split by audience (src/core2/press-money.ts); the standing outside payment is deleted. Shown in src/core2/press-money.test.ts (pool item gov-press-outlet-revenue).

whatItFakes: Where a town's readers and advertisers pay an outlet less than its people in the town cost, the town's outside customers pay it the rest each press week, in advance, as the outlet's audience elsewhere. Whether that wider audience covers the gap, or the outlet cuts its staff and may close as real papers do, is the owner's call.
why: Most towns' papers and stations are bureaus of an outlet that serves a wider area; the game models only the town's own payers, and no ruling says what happens when they fall short.
replacement: The owner's ruling on an outlet whose town pays less than its people cost (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md).

whatItFakes: An outlet's books carry its people's pay and no other costs: no printing, broadcast, rent or supplier contracts.
why: The press records an outlet's staff; its nonpayroll costs have no data yet.
replacement: An outlet's nonpayroll costs from a sourced cost structure for newspapers and stations, as supplier contracts on its books.

whatItFakes: An interview's answers carry the conversation's moves (plain, further, turn, brief) and the lie as record data, but the screen does not yet open the interview through the director's conversation, so the player cannot see the reporter's questions as spoken lines or pick a move from worded choices.
why: The conversation engine and its word banks are being rewritten by the words session (PR #4156); interview lines need its mined banks and adapters. Resolved: Oct 29, 2026 (Words session, owner: interviews are scenes). A yes to an outlet's invitation puts interview-accepted on the record (press.ts), the director stages the interview-sitting scene from it, and the conversation engine plays it (src/director/sitting.ts, with the interview's part in src/director/interview-sitting.ts): the reporter puts each of the interview's own questions as a line from the conversation bank, the player picks plain, further, turn or brief (or the lie where a vote of theirs allows one, or says nothing), and the sitting's end calls answerInterview with exactly those moves. The immediate platform answer on a yes is removed; the filed platform fills only a question the reporter could not put in words. Shown in src/director/interview-sitting.test.ts (a drawn place and seed each run).
replacement: An interview subject in the director's conversation: the reporter asks each question as a line, the four moves and the lie are the player's choices, and the chosen move is passed to answerInterview.

whatItFakes: Readers of a printed story learn which outlet printed what (the perceived fact printed:<outlet>:story), which bring-it-up's matcher reads, but bring-it-up's data has no change row for a printed story yet, so no one says it aloud.
why: The director's data belongs to the words session until PR #4156 lands; the row needs mined lines for the subject. Resolved Oct 16 (gov-stopgap-press-desk-missing-record): bring-it-up-rows.json has a news.read change row for a printed story, with bank lines naming the outlet and the topic, and a reader who read it says it aloud.
replacement: A change row {eventKind news.read, institutionFact printed: / :story} in bring-it-up-rows.json with mined lines naming the outlet, the topic and whether it ended something.

whatItFakes: A press person who lives outside the town (a station group's owner, a station news director, a national outlet's staff), or one the town had no jobless adult of the role's age left to fill in, is seated from a recorded identity in a household of one with no kin. Since people-press-staff-households they carry the one-person household officials get (official-living.ts: the Consumer Expenditure basket and the state's studio rent, and the savings a family keeps at their pay) and spend it each week, but no household record holds them a home, a family or a rent of their own. The town's own staff are filled in from its wider population with their household.
why: The identity fill-in (OPUS-CORE) seats a named person without a home or a budget; a press person's home and family need the population builder's household draw.
replacement: A press person's household drawn as the opening draws any household of their age and pay in the town, with its rent, living costs and kin.

whatItFakes: A reporter's closeness to a candidate gives access (asked first, the friendly reporter asks) and gentler copy, but a candidate cannot do a reporter a favor or leak them a story, and a reporter cannot hold a story back for a friend.
why: Favors and leaks need a player act on a reporter (a scene or a conversation move) that the director does not offer yet.
replacement: A leak as a conversation move that puts a record on the reporter's wire with the leaker named in their knowledge, and favors as relationship acts the reporter's drives and closeness read.

whatItFakes: Outlets never endorse a candidate in an editorial.
why: The decision register (docs/coordination/DECISION-REGISTER.md, 'Many ways to win') names endorsements among the channels of campaign support, so an outlet's endorsement is in; it is not built yet.
replacement: An outlet's head and owner endorse from the outlet's line, their regard for the candidates and the candidates' records, printed as a story the views and voting engines read.

whatItFakes: People of an outlet who live outside the town (every owner of a station or national outlet, a station's news director, the national tier's staff) hold no job and draw no pay, and a national outlet has no revenue or books.
why: The shared payroll path copies a schedule from a job where the employer sits, and the world keeps no full jobs outside the town; national outlets' money belongs to the national economy (OPUS-WORLD).
replacement: National outlets with books in the national economy (advertising and subscriptions by audience), paying their people through the core's payroll wherever they are based.

whatItFakes: Independent replacement hiring is removed. The masthead reads real full/counted employment and business ownership; enrollment still uses the registered SG-PEOPLE-press-employer-enrollment adapter and an endogenous replacement hire has not yet occurred in the played-year proof.
why: The invalid zero-income/reporter-owner enrollment trial was replaced by real town income anchors and the already recorded publisher. Keep this acceptance open until a jobs hire is followed to the desk in a played year; no duplicate replacement hiring remains.
replacement: The outlet's people read from its jobs: whoever the jobs engine hires into a reporter or editor position at the outlet is filled in as a named person and joins its desk; no second hiring path. Resolved Oct 16 (claude/gov-stopgap-press-faked-mechanic): a reporter or editor leaves with the job they hold and the jobs engine's hire into the opening is filled in as the outlet's new staff, followed to the desk in src/core2/press-turnover.test.ts.

whatItFakes: Only full people hold a health coverage record and pay a premium. Counted households hold none, so the wider population pays no premium and the town's health costs read as if it were uninsured.
why: The counted groups store holds no per-group plan, and a counted premium is a purchase flow with an insurer payee that fill-in must take back contract by contract (opening-customers.ts, residents.ts).
replacement: Counted households are ranked with full people by the same employer size and pay, hold a counted-coverage record on their policyholder, and pay the same premium once for each real household the record stands for (countedPayment). A household filled in is handed its counted record the same day, as full records on the same plan, policyholder and premium (onFillIn). All in src/core2/modules/coverage.ts, proved by src/core2/health-coverage-counted.test.ts.

whatItFakes: Press enrolls its already recorded owner directly in the business owner table because the shared business module has no public enrollment function for an existing owner.
why: The overnight order requires the smallest registered stand-in while the business interface is under active work; using the normal opening heuristic would incorrectly make a reporter the owner.
replacement: A shared business enrollment API accepting the existing owner and sourced books, used by press without direct table writes.

whatItFakes: A person with a cause weighs contacting only the week's shortlist of their ties (the causeHolderWeeklyContacts that pull hardest at the week's first look), not every tie every day. Whether people with causes reach out only to the people they know, ranked this way, is the owner's call (OWNER-DECISIONS.md, Open: 'Do activists reach out only to people they know?').
why: Sharing a cause ties an activist to each person told, and every tie was weighed every day, so a town's third year ran 1.35 times its first (Bedford, Wyoming); the speed rule asks that a later year run within 20 percent of the first. Built as the order's recommended version while the owner rules.
replacement: The owner's ruling on whether people with causes contact only people they know, and how many in a week (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md); then causeHolderWeeklyContacts sourced by research.

whatItFakes: Counted ballot readers still use opening stances. News now moves group stances, the press reads their population-weighted concern, and a filled-in member carries the view and story knowledge; campaign-views groupStance and saved counted ballot profiles do not yet read that heard shift.
why: The producer exposes heardShift by question. Lane 1 owns the campaign and voting readers; their narrow reader, saved-profile and cache agreement is pending in docs/lanes/agreements/1-2.md.
replacement: Wire the existing counted heardShift into the shared stance reader and saved counted ballots under agreement 1-2; prove a real story changes the background vote result in the Brookside played path.

whatItFakes: A counted group's victimizations are a tally row per place, month and group (the crime engine's tallies); the views engine moves only the full victims a crime.victimized record names, so the wider population's view on the police never moves from the crimes it lives.
why: A counted group's view is read from its opening profile alone; the views engine keeps no per-group stance a tally could move, and filling a member in would have to carry that moved view.
replacement: people-counted-victims-lived-crime: each counted group a tally row names moves its view on the police by the full victim's rule times the tally's count, citing the tally row, and a member filled in from that group holds the moved view.

whatItFakes: A couple that chose to wait carries exposure each review from the mother's age curve and the household's cushion; a whole unit is an unplanned pregnancy, and the mother weighs carrying it against ending it. Ending a pregnancy pays the trip from the household's cash to the place's outside account (no provider is paid or recorded). Counted households follow the same rule from their own record, times the households each stands for.
why: No ruling existed on what causes an unplanned pregnancy or whether the player's household can have one.
replacement: Resolved Oct 20 by the owner's ruling on #5220: unplanned pregnancies happen to people in the background from their own records and the law where they live, never to the player's own character or household, with nothing new shown to the player. The player's household is left out in renewal.ts.

whatItFakes: Only full people in couples carry exposure toward an unplanned pregnancy; the counted households, who are most of a town, have none, so the rule applies only to the full tier.
why: This change sources the trip to a provider for the full-tier rule; the counted tier's own exposure, per woman and couple times the households each record stands for, is its own piece of work.
replacement: Resolved: counted households follow the same rule from their own records, each woman carrying her own exposure times the households her record stands for, kept across fill-in (pool item people-unplanned-counted-tier, PR #5757).

whatItFakes: Miles to the nearest abortion provider are two national averages, one where the law restricts and one where it does not, not the place's own geography.
why: The core has no places-to-providers geography (Myers 2024 gives national figures only).
replacement: Resolved: the trip is read from data/research/people/abortion-provider-distance.json, Myers County-by-month travel distances to nearest abortion provider (osf.io/pfxq3), for 51 of the 56 places, with the five territories estimated and labeled (pool item people-abortion-provider-distance).

whatItFakes: The five weights of an unplanned pregnancy (renewalUnplannedExposure, renewalUnplannedAcceptance, renewalEndingBase, renewalTravelWeight, renewalTravelHalfMiles) are TUNABLE values set by hand. Their spreads are written as sensitivity windows, but no generated-year run has measured how the town's unplanned pregnancies and endings move across those windows.
why: No study publishes these as coefficients: the decision is a weighed choice from each woman's own records. Real rates (Guttmacher's about 4 unintended pregnancies a year per 100 women 15 to 44, and the share ended) can only check the town's totals, never pick a woman.
replacement: A generated-year sensitivity check in drawn places: each weight run across its window, the town's unplanned pregnancies and endings per 1,000 women 15 to 44 against the state's published rates, and each spread replaced by the measured window (pool item people-unplanned-calibration).

whatItFakes: A counted woman first seen starts with the part of a whole exposure that her years since she could first be a parent would leave at today's rate (her age curve and her household's cushion now), not the exposure her own past would have left.
why: Counted records keep no past, and starting every woman at zero would give no unplanned pregnancy for years and then the whole tier at once.
replacement: Her exposure since her last birth or partnering, read from a counted past once the opening reconstructs one (as SG-M1-opening-pregnancies does for full couples).

whatItFakes: Every conflict of interest a government's award records reaches the town's local reporters at the next weekly desk, and each weighs it in outlet and id order until one runs it. No tipster, losing bidder, clerk, disclosure form or records request brings it, and no editor assigns a beat.
why: The award is already public business on the government's books; the reporters' dig and the owner's and publisher's run decisions are the engine's own, but the paths that bring a document to a reporter (a tip from someone who knows, a request for the contract file) are not built.
replacement: A conflict reaches a reporter as a tip from the people who know of it (a losing bidder, a clerk, a colleague on the body) through the same tip path a taken bribe uses, and an editor's beat assigns the reporter who covers that government.
